reading.body:
Precision agriculture has commercial AI deployments, federal adoption data, and a UN benchmarking framework operating at the same time.

The pattern is a layered ecosystem rather than a single vendor. Deere, CNH Industrial's Raven division, and pure plays like Carbon Robotics and Monarch ship vision-guided spraying, driverless tractors, and laser weeding as farm equipment. Bayer's Climate FieldView and Corteva's Granular turn soil, weather, and yield data into planting prescriptions. Planet Labs, Descartes Labs, and EarthDaily supply the satellite imagery those models consume, while AgGateway and AEM set the data and machinery standards that make the feeds interoperable.

What makes this notable for AI is that adoption is measured, not guessed. USDA ERS publishes precision-agriculture adoption series, Census BTOS covers agriculture-adjacent sectors in its AI-use series, FAO benchmarks digital agriculture globally, and AgFunder indexes venture funding. That measurement layer means deployment can be checked against real yield and income impact rather than model demos. The data does not cover compute, power, or building constraints, and it gives no adoption percentages, revenue figures, or energy use.

summary: Precision agriculture - vision-guided spraying, yield prediction, autonomous equipment - is deployed at commercial scale. Who tracks it: federal adoption data, a UN benchmarking framework, a venture index, and standards bodies, layered over the equipment giants and AI pure-plays actually shipping it.

analysis.body:
The most concrete measure of AI use in this sector comes from the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, which covers Agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting (NAICS 11). The latest reading shows 9.5% of firms answering Yes to whether the business used AI in the last two weeks, up from 6.2% in the prior period. The series was first asked in September 2023. That is the only quantified adoption figure in the material, and it describes firms answering a survey question, not the technology itself.

What the sources describe is mostly machinery and data infrastructure rather than general-purpose AI. John Deere's precision agriculture line, including See and Spray and autonomous tractors, is presented as the reference commercial deployment. CNH Industrial's Raven division builds driverless tractor technology, AI path-planning, and precision application, the equipment layer beyond Deere. Carbon Robotics' LaserWeeder kills weeds with computer vision and lasers instead of herbicide, and Monarch builds electric driverless tractors, which the material characterizes as narrow AI shipping as farm equipment. On the software side, Bayer's Climate FieldView and Corteva's Granular are described as large digital-farming platforms turning soil, weather, and yield data into planting and input prescriptions with machine learning. Climate FieldView's own page reports that farmers using FieldView seed scripts saw an average increase of +5 bu/ac compared to users who wrote their own scripts, which is the one ROI-style figure the sources offer.

The data layer underneath these tools is where several organizations concentrate. Planet Labs supplies high-resolution satellite imagery and Earth data analytics, and the curated points describe Planet imagery alongside Descartes Labs' geospatial ML and EarthDaily's field-level crop indicators as the AI-ready observation data behind yield prediction and crop-stress detection. AgGateway, a non-profit consortium, sets open data standards that let AI models ingest feeds from tractors, drones, soil sensors, and satellites. The Association of Equipment Manufacturers covers autonomous machinery, AI hardware standards, and robotics adoption across crop and livestock production, and its page describes advocacy, safety, trade shows, and market data, including work on an EPA engine emissions proposed rule. The International Society of Precision Agriculture connects academic research on remote sensing and spatial analytics to commercial practice.

Measurement and benchmarking sit with public and international bodies. USDA's Economic Research Service publishes the data series on precision-agriculture adoption across US farms, covering variable-rate technology, yield monitoring, and autonomous equipment. The UN Food and Agriculture Organization's digital agriculture program, with the 60 Decibels-supported Digital Agriculture Index, benchmarks platform adoption and real-world yield and income impact. The FAO's e-Agriculture community facilitates dialogue on ICTs and digital innovations in agriculture, forestry, fisheries, natural resource management and rural development, and its page notes the Global AgriInno Challenge 2026 selected 13 youth-led innovation solutions from 137 valid applications out of 191 applications in total.

Money flows are tracked by AgFunder, whose research reports that global agrifoodtech funding hit $16.2 billion in 2025, almost flat versus the prior year (-3%), with investors writing checks more selectively toward companies with tangible science, real unit economics, and clear paths to revenue. AgFunder also reports that developing markets agrifoodtech funding grew substantially between 2023 and 2024 (63%) versus a 4% decline in global agrifoodtech, that APAC agrifoodtech startups raised $4.2 billion as of the end of October 2024, a 38% increase on the $3.1 billion raised over the same period in 2023, and that African agrifoodtech funding raised $145 million in the first half of 2024, a 1.6% year-over-year increase, after a 2023 decline of 62% to $275 million. The World Economic Forum's 100 Million Farmers initiative aims to move one in five of the world's farmers to regenerative and climate-smart practices by 2030, mainly by building financing and collaboration models; the material notes it does not track AI itself, but its goals around soil health, water, resilience and farmer income are the outcomes most farm AI tools claim to improve.

On risk and regulation, the sources are largely silent. AEM's page points to policy advocacy and an EPA engine emissions proposed rule, and AgGateway's traceability work is described as contributing to food safety and regulatory compliance, but no source here sets out AI-specific rules for the sector. A reader deciding whether to deploy should take from this that measured adoption remains modest at 9.5% of firms per the Census Bureau, that the commercially proven applications cluster around vision-guided spraying, autonomous equipment, and data-driven prescriptions, that the supporting infrastructure of satellite imagery, interoperability standards, and machinery standards is already institutionalized, and that the reported returns, such as the +5 bu/ac figure from Climate FieldView, come from vendors describing their own products rather than independent evaluation.

https://climate.com/.brief: Climate FieldView describes itself as an all-in-one digital farming solution for making data-driven decisions, with a separate version built for dealers that combines field data with their expertise. The page states that farmers using FieldView seed scripts saw an average increase of +5 bu/ac compared with users who wrote their own scripts. It also describes FieldView Drive 2.0, which it says can send seed scripts without a thumb drive, has built-in GPS, syncs data faster and works with a wider range of equipment. Other parts of the page point to farmer case studies, support for field trials, and planning checklists.

https://www.aem.org/.brief: AEM describes itself as an association that advances construction and agriculture equipment manufacturers in the global marketplace, and says it works across four areas: advocacy, safety, trade shows and events, and market data. It says it owns and organizes events that connect members with customers worldwide, and that its advocacy work covers grassroots campaigns, public affairs and research. AEM states it is holding a Momentum event in 2026 in Gainesville, GA, intended to deepen connections and deliver industry insights. It also says thousands of industry peers subscribe to its Industry Advisor publication for updates about equipment manufacturing.

https://www.ispag.org/.brief: The International Society of Precision Agriculture is a scientific organization that develops technologies to help feed the world and improve quality of life. It offers a definition of precision agriculture in more than fifteen languages and gives members access to directories, networking, and discounted conference registration. Members receive a monthly “ISPA newsletter” that shares news, job listings, and event information, and the society is preparing for the 17th ICPA and 11th ConBAP in summer 2026. Country Representatives promote ISPA worldwide; applicants must email info@ispag.org with a bio, CV, and be current members, and members can post job announcements on the site and in newsletters.

https://www.planet.com/.brief: Planet Labs offers a platform called Planet Insights that brings together daily satellite imagery, derived data products, and cloud-based tools in one place. The company claims its imagery is the highest-frequency commercial Earth observation data, enabling daily monitoring, high-resolution tasking, and deeper derived insights. It says the platform lets users view the planet in time, space, and frequency, helping them make decisions quickly and confidently. Planet reports that organizations across many sectors use the platform to address operational challenges with a global, dynamic perspective.

https://www.ers.usda.gov/.brief: The Economic Research Service publishes State Fact Sheets covering population, income, poverty, food security, education, employment, farm characteristics, farm financial indicators, top commodities and agricultural exports, according to the agency, with data for all states, metro and nonmetro breakouts within states, and Puerto Rico where applicable, plus county-level links where available. It also offers a Food Price Outlook with food price data and forecasts of changes in the Consumer Price Index and Producer Price Index for food. A separate Vegetables and Pulses Data collection provides statistics on fresh and processed vegetables and dry pulses in the United States, along with some global data for those sectors. The service says readers can subscribe to an e-mail notification service for announcements of its latest reports and other news.

https://agfunder.com/research/.brief: AgFunder reports that global agrifoodtech funding reached $16.2 billion in 2025, down 3% year-over-year, with investors becoming more selective and favoring companies demonstrating "tangible science, real unit economics, and clear paths to revenue." While overall funding remained relatively flat, regional patterns diverged significantly: developing markets agrifoodtech grew 63% between 2023 and 2024, Asia-Pacific startups raised $4.2 billion as of October 2024 (a 38% increase), and African agrifoodtech showed mild recovery with $145 million raised in the first half of 2024 after a 62% decline in 2023. These trends suggest a sector undergoing consolidation, with capital concentrating in regions and companies meeting stricter investment criteria.

https://www.fao.org/digital-agriculture/.brief: The page reports that the Global AgriInno Challenge 2026 finished its first stage, with 13 youth-led innovation solutions chosen from 137 valid applications out of 191 total, earning a place in a final pitch event in China. It describes e-Agriculture as a global community of practice for dialogue and information exchange on using information and communication technologies for sustainable agriculture and rural development, and states that it grew out of Action Line C7 of the World Summit on the Information Society, with the Food and Agriculture Organization assigned as facilitator. The page also notes that the FAO joined coffee value chain leaders in Geneva for the 8th CEOs & Global Leaders Forum of the International Coffee Organization, contributing to a session on collective data initiatives.
